prize_parts.citation: For introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and thereby showing how reallocation across firms shapes exporting, foreign investment and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My configuration is unchanged: B001 alone, Helpman and Melitz. What changed is the wording of the citation and how I defend it. The discovery is a framework in which firms differ in productivity and select into exporting and foreign investment, so that trade reallocates activity across firms and adds a channel to the gains from trade. Melitz (2003) and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) supplied the selection model and the exports-versus-FDI sorting result. The predictions were tested repeatedly in firm-level data, and where the baseline failed in detail the literature extended it and kept the selection logic. The papers are more than twenty years old. As a macroeconomist who works with heterogeneous-agent models, I also see the framework's reach into growth, productivity and reallocation analysis. That is secondary to the change it made in what trade economics models. Eleven files prefer the same configuration, and I do not treat that as evidence. Two of the chair's questions bear on my vote. First, the citation should name selection and reallocation and should not claim settled welfare magnitudes or the whole firm-level and quantitative trade literature. Second, I do not see a feasible two-part prize. B001 uses two of three places, so a second part could carry one person at most. A single name from B006, such as Pakes, would fragment the BLP credit, and I would not do that to fill the cap.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum made parallel contributions on exporter premia and on the Eaton-Kortum framework, and none of them is credited on this ballot entry. The Committee can only credit the names on the entry. If it reads the discovery as the empirical facts plus the theory, a two-name award is narrow, and Enflo is right that this is a judgement about what counts as the discovery and the record does not settle it. I still read the discovery as the selection and reallocation mechanism, which the citation names. The empirical precursors can be acknowledged in the scientific background. A second concern is that the baseline model's welfare implications depend on distributional and functional-form assumptions, and some of its sharper predictions are rejected. The lasting contribution is the framework and its extensions, and the citation should say so. B006 has cleaner BLP attribution and large applied reach, and I put its remaining weakness in discovery boundary and in reliance on functional-form and instrument assumptions, not in maturity. Whether a conceptual reorientation outweighs a mature toolkit is a judgement and not a theorem, and a colleague who weights tool-building equally could reasonably vote differently.

responses.point: Hassler moved from B006 first in the opening to B001 first, citing mainly the sharper discovery boundary and cleaner credit story. He keeps B006 as his first alternative. He also notes that the five credited people across B001 and B006 exceed the three-laureate limit, and that a trimmed pairing such as Pakes alone would fragment the BLP credit.
responses.response: I agree with the feasibility point and treat it as settling the structure. A combined B001 plus B006 prize cannot be built within three people without a fragmenting cut, so the choice is between them. I would put the boundary question to the Committee, and it is the one that would most move me toward B006. If demand estimation (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) can be separated defensibly from the dynamic-games strand, B006's weakness narrows. The other evidence that would move me is out-of-sample validation, for example merger retrospectives. Without those, I stay with B001 and keep B006 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Strömberg says that calling Redding 'derivative', which was my round-1 wording, understates his quantitative and spatial work. His reason for omitting him is narrower: the work is a later extension and not the origin of the selection result. He adds that if the Committee wanted the full firm-level trade lineage, a two-name award would be vulnerable.
responses.response: I accept the correction. 'Derivative' was loose wording, and I withdraw it. Redding's quantitative and spatial work is substantial and is better described as a separate achievement, the quantitative-trade lineage (B037), which is not on this shortlist. The reason to leave him out is that the origin of selection and reallocation lies with Melitz and with Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple. I agree that the vulnerability is real if the Committee defines the discovery more broadly. Under that framing Redding's claim would rise, and the two-name configuration would have to be reconsidered. I do not adopt that framing.

responses.point: Enflo wants the citation to name selection and firm heterogeneity and say nothing generic about trade theory, so it stays distinct from the 2008 recognition. She says the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum omission is not just a caveat and depends on a judgement about what counts as the discovery. She also holds B034 as an alternative, noting that the 2022 overlap cuts both ways.
responses.response: I agree with the wording point, and the citation above follows it. It names selection across heterogeneous firms and reallocation, and it makes no claim about welfare magnitudes. I also agree that the omission cannot be waved away. My answer is the one I gave above: the prize recognises the model that organised the facts and created the new welfare channel, and the precursors belong in the background. On B034 I agree that a narrow citation tied to the dynamic collateral-constraint mechanism would be distinguishable from 2022. I keep it as an alternative and not as a preferred part, because the empirical identification of the collateral channel is more indirect than the firm-level testing behind B001.

responses.point: Boppart did not rank B034 in his top eight, mainly because of thematic overlap with the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and because the empirical identification of the collateral channel is less direct than the theory. He would treat it as a serious alternative if the Committee does not find the overlap disqualifying.
responses.response: I take both points. The 2022 overlap is a real consideration, and I do not think it is disqualifying if the citation is narrow. Kiyotaki-Moore is a dynamic collateral-constraint mechanism, whereas the 2022 prize concerned banks and the study of financial crises. The weaker direct evidence for the collateral channel is the stronger objection, and it is why B034 stays behind B001 and B006 for me. It remains my second alternative because the two-person attribution is clean. I do not claim it should displace B006.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads the discovery narrowly as selection and reallocation, or broadly as the firm-level and quantitative trade programme, and whether that changes who is credited. Under the broader reading, Redding's claim and the exclusion of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum would carry more weight.
How far the sensitivity of the baseline model's welfare implications to distributional assumptions should limit the citation. I have worded it to avoid any claim about the size of the gains.

Whether the B006 discovery can be bounded to demand estimation (Berry, Levinsohn, Pakes) and how Bresnahan, Reiss, Benkard and Levin would be treated. If so, B006 is a legitimate competitor to B001 on tool-building with demonstrated reach.
How much of Helpman's credit overlaps with the monopolistic-competition lineage recognised in 2008, and how to package his work given B047, which is not on the shortlist.
My assessment rests on the supplied openings, the round-1 files and general knowledge. I have not independently verified citations, priority claims or award history.
statement.conflict_note: No connection to the B001 credited names (Helpman, Melitz, Redding) is apparent from my supplied profile. I serve as Secretary of the Committee, and I do not treat that role as evidence about any candidate. My profile lists Timo Boppart, a co-opted member, as a repeat co-author, including on the 2018 Myrdal Prize article, and John Hassler, the chair, as a long-term co-author. Neither is a credited name on B001, B006 or B034. My long-term co-authors, including Anthony Smith, José-Víctor Ríos-Rull, Giovanni Violante, Jeremy Greenwood, Zvi Hercowitz, Aleh Tsyvinski and Conny Olovsson, are macroeconomists not credited on those entries. My own field of dynamic macro and heterogeneous-agent models is adjacent to the reallocation literature the B001 framework fed, and that proximity may bias my view of its reach. I disclose these ties and do not adjudicate them.
